What Is an SR-22?

If the Virginia DMV has told you that you need an SR-22, you probably have questions — starting with what the term even means. Here's the short version: an SR-22 is not a type of insurance policy. It's a certificate your insurance company files with the state confirming that you carry the minimum liability coverage Virginia requires. Think of it as proof, not a product.

Why It's Called Financial Responsibility

In Virginia, the formal requirement is known as Financial Responsibility Certification. Once your insurer files it, the state has documented evidence that you're carrying valid coverage. If that coverage lapses for any reason, your insurance company is required to notify the DMV immediately, which triggers another suspension. That's part of why SR-22 policies tend to cost more than standard coverage — insurers are taking on additional reporting responsibility and insuring a driver the state has flagged as higher risk.

According to Virginia DMV's official SR-22 filing requirements, an SR-22 filing begins on the date the DMV receives the certificate, and drivers must maintain the filing for the entire period required — even if they don't own a car. That last part surprises a lot of people, which is why we built a dedicated non-owner insurance guide explaining how coverage works if you don't currently have a vehicle.

Who Actually Needs One

Not every driver needs an SR-22. The state typically requires the filing after:

  • An uninsured motor vehicle suspension or crash
  • Unsatisfied judgments following an accident
  • Failure to provide proof of insurance during monitoring
  • Falsifying insurance certification with the DMV
  • Certain felony or serious traffic-related license suspensions

If you've received a notice from the DMV mentioning "financial responsibility" or "SR-22," that's your cue to start shopping for a policy that includes the filing service. (Note: for DUI convictions in Virginia, an FR-44 filing with double liability limits is generally required instead of an SR-22). Our step-by-step Virginia filing process page lays out the exact steps, from choosing a provider to confirming the DMV accepted your filing.

How Long You'll Need to Keep It

In Virginia, drivers are typically required to carry an SR-22 for three continuous years. It's critical to maintain continuous coverage during this period — even a brief lapse can restart the clock or trigger a new suspension. This is one of the biggest reasons drivers work with a specialist rather than trying to piece together coverage on their own: missing a renewal date by even a day can undo months of compliance.

SR-22 vs. Regular Auto Insurance

An SR-22 policy still functions like normal auto insurance — you're covered for liability, and depending on the policy, potentially collision and comprehensive coverage too.
